It is also cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37, *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*) [SuttaCentral]. None of the secondary literature excerpts in the search dossier discuss this text directly, instead addressing unrelated homonymous figures (such as the female wanderer Sundarī murdered by heretics in the *Udāna*, Nanda's wife Sundarī, or the nun Sundarī Nandā) or medieval Indian treatises bearing the name *Sundarī*.
SuttaCentral records extensive passage-level parallels across canonical Pali collections and other Buddhist traditions [SuttaCentral]. In Pali literature, shared verses or passages connect Thig 13.4 to the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 191), the *Aṭṭhipuñja Sutta* of the *Itivuttaka* (Iti 24 / It 1.24), the *Puggalasutta* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (SN 15.10), the *Vaṅgīsattheragāthā* (Thag 21.1), and other poems of the *Therīgāthā* (Thig 7.2, Thig 7.3, and Thig 13.3) [SuttaCentral]. Sanskrit and Chinese parallels include the *Divyāvadāna*, the *Udānavarga* (UV 27 and Tibetan Uv Kg 27), and Chinese translations of the *Dharmapada* and related anthologies (T 210.22, T 212.28, and T 213.27) [SuttaCentral].
Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms pervasive reproduction of the poem (§0.3–26.5) in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as specific verse matches (§9.4–10.4) shared with the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* and *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Across languages, DharmaNexus aligns passages with the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094) and the *Śrīmanmahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotra* (D1153), the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, and Chinese Āgama translations including the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100), *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), and *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
